title: The Second Rejection Letter
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] The first rejection stung, but the second one, arriving almost exactly a year later, felt disproportionately worse, as though I hadn't grown at all in the interim.
Narrator: I'd spent that year overhauling my research proposal, incorporating feedback I'd practically begged a reviewer to give me, and still it wasn't enough.
Narrator: [carefully] For a few weeks afterward, I genuinely considered abandoning the whole idea, telling myself that some doors are closed for a reason, however tempting that explanation was.
Narrator: What eventually pulled me out of that spiral wasn't encouragement, oddly enough, but irritation, the sense that I was letting one committee's opinion define my entire trajectory.
Narrator: [reflective] So I did something I probably should have done the first time: I emailed three professors whose work I actually understood, rather than simply admired from a distance.

Narrator: One of them, to my surprise, replied within a day and pointed out that my proposal had been trying to answer three questions at once, which is rarely well received by an admissions committee.
Narrator: [honestly] It's humbling to be told, essentially, that your ambition was mistaken for a lack of focus, though I suppose that's precisely what had happened.
Narrator: I narrowed the proposal down to a single, tightly argued question, even though it meant discarding months of work I'd grown attached to.
Narrator: [gently] Whether this version gets accepted remains to be seen, but I no longer feel like I'm gambling on something vague and unexamined.
Narrator: I've also stopped conflating rejection with unworthiness, a distinction that sounds obvious until you're the one sitting with the actual letter.
Narrator: [calmly] A mentor once told me that being overlooked twice doesn't make a person any less capable, only less lucky in timing, and I've come to believe she was right.

Narrator: Whatever happens with this application, the process has forced me to articulate, precisely, what I actually want to spend the next five years investigating, and that alone feels like it was worth the discomfort.
